questions.q: What interval units does bin() accept, beyond the single 1h example from Lesson 24?
options: Any duration — minutes (m), hours (h), days (d), chosen based on the actual practical need
Only 1-hour intervals, with no other option
Only whole-day intervals
bin() does not accept a configurable interval at all
questions.explain: 5-minute buckets fit a live dashboard tracking the last hour; daily buckets fit a trend chart spanning months.

questions.q: What does ago(1h) mean in a KQL query?
options: One hour before the moment the query actually runs — a moving reference point, not a fixed timestamp
Exactly one specific, fixed calendar timestamp
One hour after the query runs
A synonym for bin(pickup_time, 1h)
questions.explain: This recalculates automatically every time the query runs, keeping a dashboard's "last hour" view current.

questions.q: Why might make-series show a bucket that summarize ... by bin(...) would have silently omitted?
options: make-series explicitly fills in every interval in a range, including zero-count intervals with no events at all, unlike summarize/bin which only returns buckets that have data
make-series and summarize/bin produce identical results in every case
make-series only works on buckets that already have data, same as summarize
summarize/bin always includes every interval automatically
questions.explain: A missing bucket on a real chart would otherwise look like missing data rather than a genuine zero.

questions.q: Why are bin(), ago(), and make-series described as the real reason a KQL Database exists?
options: They're first-class time-series operations that a general-purpose DataFrame engine or T-SQL can't express nearly as directly or efficiently at scale
They have no real connection to why KQL Databases are optimized differently
These functions are actually available identically in T-SQL
They only matter for batch processing, not streaming
questions.explain: This connects directly to Lesson 21's point about KQL Databases being optimized differently from Delta tables.

questions.q: What does the where pickup_time > ago(1h) query pattern power on a real dashboard?
options: "Show me everything from the last hour" — automatically staying current every time the query runs
A one-time historical snapshot from a fixed past date
A query that never actually returns any results
A query that only works with make-series, not where
questions.explain: This is the real mechanism behind Lesson 28's live dashboards.
